title: Whether the pause before a plausible answer can be taught
scenario_source_text: You asked what a curriculum has to teach differently if the danger is a plausible answer arriving too early. I think the answer is you teach the pause — deliberately not acting on the first plausible draft. But I'm not sure a pause can be taught.

exchanges.contribution: You asked what a curriculum has to teach differently if the danger is a plausible answer arriving too early. I think the answer is you teach the pause — deliberately not acting on the first plausible draft. But I'm not sure a pause can be taught.
exchanges.response: Say more about 'can't be taught'. When you personally learned to distrust a too-easy answer, what did it — a person, a failure, a habit you were made to repeat? Name the mechanism, then we can ask whether a curriculum can reproduce it.

exchanges.contribution: Honestly it was shipping something that tested well in the room and then failed with real users. The gap between plausible and right stopped being abstract.
exchanges.response: So your teacher was a consequence you couldn't argue away. What is the closest a studio course can get to that consequence without waiting for a real product to fail?
